```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(survey)
df <- read_csv("data/wellbeing_2024_clean.csv")
des <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~final_wt, data = df)
```

# Overview

The 2024 wellbeing survey ran from 4 to 29 March. It was sent to all
enrolled students, and `r nrow(df)` completed responses were received,
a response rate of `r scales::percent(nrow(df) / 18450, accuracy = 0.1)`.
Results below are weighted to the student population by faculty, level
of study and sex.

Wellbeing was measured with the short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental
Wellbeing Scale [SWEMWBS, @stewartbrown2009], which has seven items
scored 1--5. Raw totals were converted to metric scores using the
published conversion table, giving a range of 7.00 to 35.00.

# Overall wellbeing

```{r overall}
m <- svymean(~swemwbs_metric, des, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The weighted mean SWEMWBS score was `r round(coef(m), 1)` (SE
`r round(SE(m), 2)`). This is slightly below the 2022 figure and about
two points below published population norms for adults of a similar
age [@ng2017, p. 3].

```{r fig-dist, fig.cap="Distribution of SWEMWBS metric scores, weighted.", fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(df, aes(x = swemwbs_metric, weight = final_wt)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "SWEMWBS metric score", y = "Weighted count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Differences between groups

```{r by-group}
by_level <- svyby(~swemwbs_metric, ~level, des, svymean, na.rm = TRUE)
by_level
```

Postgraduate research students reported the lowest mean scores, and
first-year undergraduates the highest. The gap between them is about
`r round(diff(range(coef(by_level))), 1)` points.

| Group                    | Mean | 95% CI       |
|:-------------------------|-----:|:-------------|
| Undergraduate, year 1    | 22.4 | 22.0 -- 22.8 |
| Undergraduate, year 2+   | 21.6 | 21.3 -- 21.9 |
| Taught postgraduate      | 21.9 | 21.4 -- 22.4 |
| Research postgraduate    | 20.8 | 20.1 -- 21.5 |

: Weighted mean SWEMWBS score by level of study.

The differences are modest in size. A difference of three points is
sometimes treated as the minimal important difference for individuals
[@shah2018], and none of the group differences reaches that.

# Item-level results

```{r items, fig.cap="Percentage answering 'often' or 'all of the time' to each item.", echo=FALSE}
items <- df |>
  select(starts_with("swem_")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(pct = weighted.mean(value >= 4, w = df$final_wt, na.rm = TRUE))
ggplot(items, aes(x = pct, y = reorder(name, pct))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

The item with the lowest endorsement was "I've been feeling relaxed",
endorsed 'often' or 'all of the time' by only about a quarter of
respondents. This mirrors the 2022 results.

# Notes on method

- Missing item responses were not imputed. Respondents missing more
  than one item were excluded from the scale score
  (`r sum(is.na(df$swemwbs_metric))` cases).
- Weights were trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles.
- Confidence intervals use the Taylor linearisation variance estimator
  from the **survey** package [@lumley2004].
